messages.text: Look, I've had the place appraised and the market's moved up considerably since your lease started. I'm looking at twenty-four hundred a month going forward.

I appreciate you sharing that, but I need to pump the brakes here—that's a jump from eighteen hundred, right? That's a third increase in one year. Before we talk numbers, can you walk me through what's actually driving this? Are you saying the market really shifted that much, or are there specific costs on your end that went up?

Yeah, the market's definitely shifted—I've got comparable units in the building going for twenty-five, twenty-six hundred. My property taxes went up, insurance is through the roof, and frankly, I can't absorb those costs myself if I want to keep this place maintained the way it is.

Okay, that's helpful context. I get that your costs went up—that's real. But here's the thing: I've also looked at comps in the area, and I'm seeing twenty-one to twenty-two for units like mine, not twenty-five. And those higher ones are newer or have amenities I don't have. Can you show me which listings you're looking at? Because if we're basing this on actual market data, we should be working from the same numbers.

Look, I'm not going to sit here and compare listings with you all day—I know what units are going for, and twenty-four hundred is fair market rate for what you've got. You're a good tenant, I don't want to lose you, but I've got other people ready to sign at that number if you walk.

I hear you, and I value that you want to keep me around. But here's what doesn't add up: if there are people lined up to sign at twenty-four hundred, why are we negotiating? That tells me there's some real interest in keeping this continuity too. Look, I'm not trying to lowball you—I just need numbers that work for both of us. What if we broke this down: what are your actual cost increases year-over-year? Property tax, insurance, maintenance?

My costs aren't really up for debate here—that's my business. What matters is what the market will bear, and right now it'll bear twenty-four hundred. If you want to stay, that's the number. I'd rather keep you than deal with turnover, but I'm not going to leave money on the table just because we get along.

I understand you've got real costs, and I'm not asking you to take a loss. But you can't have it both ways—you can't say the market rate is twenty-four hundred and also say you'd rather keep me than deal with turnover. Those two things are in tension. Here's what I'm proposing: let's find a number that acknowledges your legitimate cost increases without pricing me out of my own apartment. What if we split the difference and looked at twenty-two hundred, with a clearer picture of what those actual increases were?

Twenty-two hundred is too low—that doesn't cover what I need. Look, I get the appeal of that number, but I'm not coming down that far. I could maybe do twenty-three fifty if you sign for two years instead of one, but that's about as much room as I've got.

Twenty-three fifty for two years—okay, that's movement, and I appreciate that. But I need to be straight with you: locking in for two years when we're already talking about a nineteen percent jump puts all the risk on me if things change. What's driving the two-year ask? Is it just to lock in the higher rate, or is there actual cost certainty on your end that makes two years valuable to you?

It's both—yeah, I want the stability of a longer lease, but it also lets me plan better knowing I've got consistent income. Look, two years at twenty-three fifty is a solid deal for you compared to the market. That's my best offer without you giving me something real in return.

Okay, I hear that. Two-year stability makes sense for you. But here's what I'd want in return for that commitment: twenty-three fifty for year one, then a smaller bump—say three percent—for year two. That way you've got your planning certainty, I'm not taking all the risk, and we're both anchored to something objective instead of whatever the market might do. Does that framework work for you?

No, that doesn't work—that's just kicking the can down the road and leaving me guessing on year two. I need twenty-three fifty flat for the full two years, take it or leave it. That's where I'm at, and honestly, I've already bent further than I wanted to get you to stay.

I hear you, and I'm genuinely trying to find middle ground here. But flat twenty-three fifty for two years means zero adjustment for your costs in year two, which you just said you need planning certainty for—those don't match up. Here's my counter: twenty-two seventy-five flat for two years. It's closer to covering your increases than where we started, you get your locked-in income, and it's actually reasonable on both sides. What do you think?

Twenty-two seventy-five isn't going to cut it—that's basically back where we started before I even moved. Look, I've given you twenty-three fifty, which is a real number, and I'm not chipping away at it anymore. You want to stay or not?

I do want to stay—I like this place and I've been a reliable tenant. But I also can't ignore that twenty-three fifty is still a fifteen percent increase on an eighteen-month timeline, and you're asking me to lock that in for two years with no flexibility. Let me ask directly: is there any number between twenty-three fifty and twenty-three that would actually work for you, or are we genuinely at an impasse here?

Look, I could go to twenty-three hundred flat for two years, but that's it—I'm not going lower than that. That's my final number, and if you want to stay, we need to get this done this week before I start showing to other people.

Twenty-three hundred for two years—I can work with that. That's a thirteen percent increase overall, which is steep but at least it's spread across two years and it gives us both some certainty. Before I commit, I just want to confirm: that's twenty-three hundred flat both years, no additional increases, and we're locked in through the end of year two, right?
Yeah, that's right—twenty-three hundred flat for the full two years, no increases, lease runs through the end of year two. I'll have the paperwork drawn up tomorrow. You good with that?
